Desk guide

  
Your first round
  1. Start round opens your desk. Each customer arrives five simulated seconds after the last. Next order lets you go one at a time.
  2. Your bid is what you pay to buy. Your ask is what you charge to sell. A customer who sells leaves you holding shares.
  3. Change the half spread or price shift, then select Post quote. The new settings apply from the next order. Both prices follow the public reference.
  4. At the end, open the Replay room. Choose a trade, change the quote, and see the effect on your final profit.

  
Why lower both prices?
If you already own a lot of shares, a lower bid makes you a less attractive buyer. A lower ask can help you sell. Your rival can still beat either price.

  
Reading the chart
The line tracks the public reference. Bars show shares traded per order, colored by the customer’s side. Dots mark your fills. Hover over the chart, or focus it and use the arrow keys, to read a time, price, and volume.
How the exchange works
Each order is a request for a price. An eligible dealer must meet the customer’s private limit. The best price wins first, and a seeded coin toss breaks ties. Your quote size refreshes on each order. The rival can take any eligible remainder. Inventory is capped at 1,000 shares in either direction.

  
How profit is counted
Profit equals cash from trading plus the value of your shares. A short position is a negative share count. Each share you trade costs one cent in fees. Buying 100 shares at $99.95 and selling them at $100.05 earns $10 before fees and $8 after fees.
During the round, shares are valued at the public reference. At the close, the simulator reveals the final underlying value and uses it to value your remaining position. The final mark is a valuation, not a sale.

  
What the seed does
The seed is the number used to generate the market. Reusing it recreates the same customers, hidden values, and rival quotes. Your own fills depend on what you post. Five minutes of opening history gives you price and order context before your desk opens.

  
Research limits
One fictional stock trades against one rival. Your trades do not move the underlying price. There is no borrowing cost, network delay, or queue beyond the seeded tie break. Tournament results describe this simulated market.
